When New Orleans was founded in 1718, the entire city was above sea level. Over half the city is now below sea level. This sinking, known as subsidence, was primarily caused by human engineering.
Today, while neighborhoods built on the original higher ground (such as the French Quarter) remain safely elevated, many areas established in the 20th century sit in sunken "bowls" that range from 3 to 12 feet below sea level.
New Orleans, Louisiana: Poised for high-tide flooding issues and potential land loss.
[Miami, Florida: Expected to face chronic high-tide flooding on a near-daily basis by 2050.
[Charleston, South Carolina: Projected to experience a significant jump in flood days by 2050.
[New York City, New York: Increased exposure of residential units and infrastructure to floodwaters.
[San Francisco & Bay Area, California: Potential for significant flooding around low-lying coastal areas and airports.
[Virginia Beach, Virginia: High-risk areas facing both sea-level rise and land subsidence.  
These projections are often based on research from organizations like Climate Central's sea level rise maps, which use satellite data to measure land elevation against projected sea-level changes.

LIFESTYLE
New Orleans was built above sea level, but the sinking city tries to weather Hurricane Ida
Mike Szydlowski
Updated Sept. 1, 2021, 3:03 p.m. CT
Hurricane Ida slammed into the Louisiana coast as a Category 4 hurricane Sunday with sustained winds of 150 mph. This ties the record for the strongest hurricane ever to hit the state.

Strong hurricanes are always dangerous, however, when they hit Louisiana; they are particularly dangerous because of one very popular city — New Orleans. It isn't the city's popularity that makes it dangerous, but the fact that a very large portion of the city is built below sea level.

Essentially, over half the city of New Orleans is a bowl right next to the Mississippi River, a very large lake, and the Gulf of Mexico. The question is: Why would anybody build a city on ground that is below sea level?

The answer is “They didn’t!” Here is what really happened.


Sediment created the land where New Orleans was built — above sea level
For thousands of years, the Mississippi River transported incredible amounts of sediment deposited in the Northern Plains during the last ice age. That sediment poured into the Gulf of Mexico.

As soon as the sediment hit the Gulf, it slowed down and fell to the bottom. Over time, the sediment accumulated enough to create new land that is now New Orleans.

The land continued to rise above sea level as the Mississippi River flooded every spring. Every time the river flooded, sediment was deposited, which built up the land. This continued for thousands of years and created what is now known as New Orleans — all of which was above sea level. This remained true as the city started its development stage in the 1800s.
